opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, Peter. The short version is that the brain didn't evolve to think about the distant future. For most of our history, "the future" meant tonight or tomorrow: will I find food, is there a predator behind that bush. So the machinery we have for imagining what's ahead is tuned for short horizons, and when we push it further, it starts to break down in some interesting ways.

One finding I find striking comes from imaging studies. When you ask people to think about themselves ten or twenty years from now, the brain activity looks less like thinking about yourself and more like thinking about a stranger. Your future self is, neurologically, a bit of an acquaintance. That explains a lot of behavior. Why don't people save for retirement? Why do we eat the dessert, skip the gym, put off the doctor's appointment? We're essentially asking ourselves to sacrifice for someone we don't feel deeply connected to.

The second limitation is that we imagine the future by recombining the past. The same regions that retrieve memories are the ones we use to simulate what's coming. So when you picture your life in 2050, you're really taking pieces of today and rearranging them. That's why our predictions are so often just the present with slightly better gadgets. People in the 1950s imagined flying cars, but almost nobody imagined the smartphone, because there was nothing in memory to build it from.

Third, we're poor at exponential thinking. Our intuitions are linear. If something doubles every year, the brain keeps underestimating where it ends up, whether that's technology, compound interest, or a pandemic.

And finally, there's the emotional side. We assume our future selves will want what we want now. Psychologists call it the "end of history illusion." Everyone acknowledges they changed a lot over the past ten years, but they predict they'll change very little over the next ten. We think we've arrived. We haven't.

The good news is that knowing this lets you design around it. Some of my favorite work shows that if you make the future self more vivid, by showing people an aged photo of themselves or having them write a letter from their future self, they actually save more and make better long-term decisions. You can't rewire evolution, but you can give the brain a better picture of the stranger it's going to become, so it starts treating that person like you.

r001.rationale: The response says people project current wants onto future selves and build future scenarios from past memories, but it does not state that imagining oneself in old age means projecting the present self into that age.

r002.rationale: The response discusses limits in imagining the distant future, but does not distinguish understanding age-related limitations from imagining what it would feel like to experience them.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about it is that the brain is basically a prediction machine, but it was built for a very specific kind of prediction. It evolved to answer questions like, where is the food going to be tomorrow, is that rustle in the grass a predator, will this person help me or hurt me next season. Those are short horizons. Days, months, maybe a few years. There was never any evolutionary pressure to be good at imagining what the world looks like in fifty or a hundred years, because nothing you did with that information changed whether you survived and reproduced.

And you can actually see this in the brain. When we put people in a scanner and ask them to think about themselves in a week, the areas that light up are the ones involved in self-reference, the medial prefrontal cortex, the same regions that are active when you think about yourself right now. But when you ask them to think about themselves in thirty years, the activity shifts. It starts to look more like the pattern you get when people think about a stranger. So your future self, neurologically, is kind of a different person. Which explains a lot about why we don't save for retirement, why we don't take care of our health, why climate change feels abstract. We're being asked to sacrifice for someone who, as far as the brain is concerned, isn't really us.

The other piece is that imagination isn't creation, it's recombination. When you picture the future, your brain takes memories and rearranges them. So you're always building the future out of parts of the past. That's why if you look at science fiction from the fifties, the flying cars still have fins and the computers still have knobs. People couldn't imagine the internet, not because they weren't smart, but because they had no memory fragments to build it from. The truly novel is almost invisible to us before it arrives.

And then there's a third limitation, which is that the brain compresses. Emotionally, a hundred years from now and a thousand years from now feel about the same. The discounting curve flattens out. So we're not just bad at imagining the far future, we're bad at caring about it in a calibrated way. I actually find that kind of humbling, because it means that whenever someone tells you confidently what the world will look like in 2100, what you're really hearing is their memories, slightly shuffled.

r001.rationale: The response says imagining one’s future self decades ahead resembles thinking about a stranger; it does not say imagining old age projects the present self onto an older age.

r002.rationale: It discusses difficulty identifying with a distant future self, but does not distinguish understanding age-related limitations from imagining what it is like to experience them.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the limitations is that we imagine the future using the machinery we use to remember the past. You ask me to picture my life in twenty years, and I take things I know—my home, the people around me, my work—and rearrange them. Maybe I make myself older. But that’s a projection of what I already know, and the future can contain things I don’t yet have the concepts to imagine.

There’s also a difference between understanding something intellectually and feeling it. I can understand that my decisions today will affect me decades from now. But the person who will experience those consequences can feel quite abstract, whereas whatever I want right now is vivid and immediate.

So we can talk about a distant future, put a date on it, even build a model of it, without having a very rich emotional connection to it. That’s a limitation worth recognizing: being able to describe a future doesn’t necessarily mean we can intuitively grasp what living in it will be like.

r001.rationale: It says we picture life decades ahead by rearranging things we know about ourselves and perhaps making ourselves older, describing a projection of the present self.

r002.rationale: It contrasts intellectually understanding future consequences with feeling connected to a future self, but does not address understanding age-related limitations versus imagining experiencing them.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the limitations is that when we imagine the future, we’re using material from the past. You can put yourself in a city you’ve never visited, or imagine a technology that doesn’t exist, but the pieces you’re assembling come from things you already know. So what feels like imagining something entirely new is often rearranging familiar things.

And the farther out you go, the harder that becomes. Imagine what you’ll have for breakfast tomorrow—you can probably make a fairly vivid picture. Now imagine an ordinary morning in your life forty years from now. Where are you? Who’s there? What do you care about? You can tell a story, but so many of the things that would determine that morning are unknown to you today.

The danger is that we confuse the vividness of the story with how likely it is to happen. A future that’s easy to picture can feel more plausible than one we don’t have the vocabulary for yet. So I’d treat imagination as a way to explore possible futures, while being very careful about treating it as a prediction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses imagining a morning forty years from now, but does not say that this amounts to projecting one's present self into old age.

r002.rationale: It notes that future circumstances are unknown, but does not distinguish understanding age-related limitations from imagining what it feels like to experience them.
